# What is this script about?

This is the **pilot run** for the master's thesis. The goal is not the final dataset but an
honest test of the entire pipeline on **one outlet and one month**:

1. **Find articles** via the monthly archive of tagesschau.de
2. **Fetch full texts**: download the article pages and extract the body text
3. **Clean**: remove duplicates, videos, irrelevant hits and articles outside the period
4. **Build the corpus and DTM** with `quanteda`
5. **First analyses**: dictionaries (e.g. “Genozid” (genocide), “Selbstverteidigung” (self-defence)), keywords in context
6. **Detect source attributions** at sentence level (IDF, Hamas authorities, UN, news agencies …)
7. **Template** for adding further outlets (taz, FAZ, NZZ, …) in the same format

By the end, you will know how long scraping takes, how clean the texts are and whether the
analyses can, in principle, answer the questions you care about.

> **Legal note:** Text and data mining for scientific research is generally permitted in
> Germany under § 60d UrhG (German Copyright Act). The terms of use of the tagesschau API
> allow non-commercial use but **no publication** of the content. For you, this means: do not
> circumvent paywalls, do not publish the full-text corpus (at most IDs/URLs and derived
> metrics) and scrape politely. Also clarify the details with your supervisor or the library.

# Setup

## Load packages

We need only a few packages. The chunk below installs missing packages automatically
and then loads all of them.

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `httr2` | HTTP requests to the API, including rate limiting and retries |
| `rvest` / `xml2` | Parse HTML pages, i.e. extract the article text |
| `jsonlite` | Convert API responses (JSON) into R objects |
| `dplyr`, `purrr`, `stringr`, `tibble`, `tidyr`, `readr`, `lubridate` | Data management (“tidyverse”) |
| `quanteda`, `quanteda.textstats` | Corpus, tokenisation, DTM, dictionary and keyness analyses |

```{r pakete}
pakete <- c("httr2", "rvest", "xml2", "jsonlite", "dplyr", "purrr", "stringr",
            "tibble", "tidyr", "readr", "lubridate", "quanteda", "quanteda.textstats")

fehlend <- pakete[!pakete %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(fehlend) > 0) install.packages(fehlend)

invisible(lapply(pakete, library, character.only = TRUE))
```

## Parameters: everything you want to adjust is here

All settings live in **one** place, so you do not have to search the code later when you,
for example, change the period.

- **`zeitraum_start` / `zeitraum_ende`** (period start/end): one month for the pilot.
- **`max_seiten`** (max pages): upper limit of archive pages per month (up to 140 entries each).
  Prevents endless runs.
- **`vorfilter`** (pre-filter): only fully download articles with a key term in the title or
  teaser (saves many requests, see Step 1).
- **`kontakt`** (contact): sent in the *user agent*, so site operators can see who is making
  requests and how to reach you. This is good scraping practice.
- **`neu_scrapen`** (re-scrape): if set to `FALSE`, the script uses only previously saved data.
  Useful when you only want to re-knit the analysis.

```{r parameter}
zeitraum_start <- as.Date("2023-10-07")
zeitraum_ende  <- as.Date("2023-11-07")
max_seiten     <- 15          # archive pages per month (October 2023 had 4)
vorfilter      <- TRUE
kontakt        <- "Masterarbeit (Universitaet XY), Kontakt: deine.mail@uni-xy.de"  # adjust!
neu_scrapen    <- TRUE

# Folder structure: raw data (unaltered downloads) kept separate from processed data.
# This lets you rerun any processing step without downloading again.
dir.create("data/raw/tagesschau_archiv", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("data/raw/tagesschau_html",   recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("data/processed",             recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

---

# Step 1: Find articles via the monthly archive

## Why not the search API?

The first draft used the tagesschau.de search API. The first test run showed that the search
returns **only roughly the last four weeks** (173 hits in the test, all from
September/October 2026). This makes it useless for historical windows such as October 2023.

## The monthly archive

tagesschau.de has an **archive for each month** that lists all reports, newest first:

```
https://www.tagesschau.de/archiv?datum=2023-10-01&pageIndex=1
```

- `datum` (date): always the **first day of the month** (other days also show the whole month)
- `pageIndex`: page 1, 2, 3 … with up to 140 entries each. An empty page means the month is over.
  October 2023 had 4 pages with roughly 500 entries in total.

Each entry (CSS class `teaser-right`) contains everything we need for the pre-selection:

| Field | Location in the HTML |
|---|---|
| Link to the article | `a.teaser-right__link` (attribute `href`) |
| Kicker (topline) | `.teaser-right__labeltopline` |
| Title | `.teaser-right__headline` |
| Short text (teaser) | `.teaser-right__shorttext` |
| Timestamp | attribute `data-teaserdate` (Unix time in seconds) |

We load each archive page **once**, cache it (`data/raw/tagesschau_archiv/`)
and wait 3 seconds between requests.

```{r tagesschau-archiv}
```

## Retrieve and pre-filter the archive for the period

1. Determine all months the period touches and fetch all archive pages for each month.
2. Filter to the exact period.
3. Keep **only text articles and commentaries**, i.e. digital newspaper articles. Videos, audio
   and live blogs sit under other paths (`/multimedia/`, `/newsticker/`) and are dropped.
   Live blogs are deliberately excluded from the corpus: tagesschau.de no longer hosts those from
   2023/2024, and for the other outlets they are not available via Nexis anyway. Commentaries (`/kommentar/`) stay in because they
   show the outlet's opinion section; flag them in the analysis via the `ressort` (section) column.
4. **Pre-filter:** only entries with a key term in the kicker, title or short text are
   downloaded in full later. This saves many requests. The drawback: an article that only
   takes up the topic further down in the text slips through. This is acceptable for the pilot;
   check it with `vorfilter <- FALSE` for one month if you want to know how much is lost.

```{r archiv-ausfuehren, eval = neu_scrapen}
monate <- seq(floor_date(zeitraum_start, "month"), floor_date(zeitraum_ende, "month"), by = "month")

archiv <- map_dfr(as.character(monate), monat_holen)
message(nrow(archiv), " Einträge im Archiv für ", length(monate), " Monat(e).")

vorfilter_begriffe <- regex(
  "israel|gaza|hamas|nahost|westjordanland|pal(ä|ae)stin|idf|netanjahu|geisel",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

treffer <- archiv |>
  mutate(datum = as.Date(zeit, tz = "Europe/Berlin")) |>
  filter(datum >= zeitraum_start, datum <= zeitraum_ende) |>
  filter(str_detect(url, "tagesschau\\.de/(inland|ausland|wirtschaft|investigativ|faktenfinder|wissen|kommentar)/")) |>
  mutate(
    id      = str_remove(basename(url), "\\.html$"),
    ressort = str_match(url, "tagesschau\\.de/([^/]+)/")[, 2],
    vorfilter_treffer = str_detect(paste(topline, titel, kurztext), vorfilter_begriffe)
  ) |>
  distinct(url, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Stop with a clear message if something goes fundamentally wrong
if (nrow(treffer) == 0) {
  stop("Keine Archiv-Einträge im Zeitraum. Datumsspanne im Archiv: ",
       paste(range(as.Date(archiv$zeit)), collapse = " bis "),
       ". Prüfe zeitraum_start/zeitraum_ende und ob die Archivseiten geladen wurden.")
}

message(nrow(treffer), " Textartikel im Zeitraum, davon ", sum(treffer$vorfilter_treffer),
        " mit Kernbegriff in Titel/Teaser.")
if (vorfilter) treffer <- filter(treffer, vorfilter_treffer)

write_csv(treffer, "data/processed/tagesschau_treffer_roh.csv")
```

---

# Step 2: Fetch full texts from the article pages

The archive provides only titles and teasers. We fetch the **full text** from the
article page (`url`). This is classic **web scraping** with `rvest`:

1. Download the page HTML (and cache it)
2. Use a **CSS selector** to find the paragraphs that belong to the body text
3. Extract and join the text

## How do you find the right CSS selector?

Open an article in your browser → right-click a paragraph → **“Inspect”** (“Untersuchen” in a
German browser). You will see, for example, `<p class="textabsatz">`. The matching selector is
`p.textabsatz`. Alternatively, the browser extension **SelectorGadget** helps.

> **Caution:** Websites change their HTML from time to time. If you suddenly get empty
> texts, the selector is almost always outdated. That is why there is a **fallback**
> below: if the specific selector finds nothing, we take all `<p>` elements in the
> `<article>` section.

As with the archive, we wait **3 seconds** between requests so as not to strain the
server. The selector `p.textabsatz` also works for articles from 2023 (checked).

```{r tagesschau-volltext}
```

```{r volltext-ausfuehren, eval = neu_scrapen}
zu_holen <- read_csv("data/processed/tagesschau_treffer_roh.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

message(nrow(zu_holen), " Artikel werden geholt, geschätzte Dauer: ~",
        round(nrow(zu_holen) * 3.5 / 60), " Minuten")

zu_holen$html_datei <- map2_chr(zu_holen$id, zu_holen$url, html_holen, .progress = TRUE)
zu_holen$text       <- map_chr(zu_holen$html_datei, text_extrahieren)

write_csv(zu_holen, "data/processed/tagesschau_artikel_roh.csv")
```

---

# Step 3: Cleaning

Raw data are never clean. Typical problems and how we address them:

| Problem | Solution |
|---|---|
| Text is empty (selector did not match, page offline) | Drop articles with < 300 characters and record the count |
| Article touches the Middle East only marginally (e.g. domestic politics with one subordinate clause on Israel) | **Relevance filter**: key terms must occur at least twice |
| Live blogs / tickers | do not belong in the corpus; already excluded via the path in Step 1, the `liveblog` column is only a safety net |
| Uniform format for multiple outlets | fixed columns: `medium, id, url, datum, titel, text` (outlet, ID, URL, date, title, text) |

You should **validate** the relevance filter later: read 50 filtered-out and 50 retained
articles and check whether the decision is correct. This also belongs in the thesis.

```{r bereinigung}
kernbegriffe <- regex(
  "israel|gaza|hamas|nahost|westjordanland|pal(ä|ae)stin|idf|hisbollah|netanjahu",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

artikel <- read_csv("data/processed/tagesschau_artikel_roh.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    medium        = "tagesschau",
    text          = coalesce(text, ""),
    n_zeichen     = nchar(text),
    n_kernbegriff = str_count(paste(titel, text), kernbegriffe),
    liveblog      = str_detect(paste(titel, url), regex("liveblog|ticker", ignore_case = TRUE))
  )

# Transparency: how many articles are dropped at which step?
tibble(
  schritt = c("Treffer im Zeitraum (Stories)", "davon mit Text >= 300 Zeichen",
              "davon relevant (>= 2 Kernbegriffe)"),
  n = c(nrow(artikel),
        sum(artikel$n_zeichen >= 300),
        sum(artikel$n_zeichen >= 300 & artikel$n_kernbegriff >= 2))
)

artikel <- artikel |>
  filter(n_zeichen >= 300, n_kernbegriff >= 2) |>
  select(medium, id, url, datum, titel, topline, ressort, liveblog, text)

if (nrow(artikel) == 0) {
  stop("Nach der Bereinigung ist kein Artikel übrig. Häufigste Ursache: Der Text-Selektor ",
       "greift nicht mehr (alle Texte < 300 Zeichen). Prüfe eine Datei in data/raw/tagesschau_html/.")
}

write_csv(artikel, "data/processed/korpus_tagesschau.csv")
```

# Step 4: Corpus and document-term matrix (DTM)

## What happens here?

A computer cannot “read” texts. We therefore translate them into numbers:

1. **Corpus**: texts plus metadata (outlet, date, …) in one object
2. **Tokens**: split texts into individual words
3. **Clean**: remove punctuation, numbers, URLs and **stop words** (“der”, “und”, “ist” – “the”,
   “and”, “is”), and lowercase everything
4. **DTM** (in `quanteda`: *dfm*): a matrix with **one row per article** and
   **one column per word**. The cells count how often the word occurs in the article.

This matrix is **sparse**: the vast majority of cells are 0 because each article uses only
a small part of the total vocabulary. `quanteda` stores only the non-zero values; otherwise
memory would fill up quickly.

**Multi-word expressions** such as “israelische Armee” (Israeli army) or “Vereinte Nationen”
(United Nations) would fall apart during tokenisation. `tokens_compound()` merges them into
a single token (`israelische_armee`).

```{r korpus-dtm}
korp <- corpus(artikel, docid_field = "id", text_field = "text")
# Also store the article ID as metadata: we need it later
# when we split the texts into sentences (Step 6).
docvars(korp, "artikel_id") <- docnames(korp)
summary(korp, n = 5)

mehrwort <- phrase(c("israelische armee", "israelische streitkräfte", "vereinte nationen",
                     "rotes kreuz", "human rights watch", "amnesty international",
                     "internationaler gerichtshof", "zwei-staaten-lösung"))

toks <- tokens(korp,
               remove_punct   = TRUE,
               remove_numbers = TRUE,
               remove_url     = TRUE,
               remove_symbols = TRUE) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_compound(mehrwort) |>
  tokens_remove(c(stopwords("de"), "sagte", "sei", "seien", "worden", "dass", "mehr",
                  "tagesschau", "uhr"))

dtm_voll <- dfm(toks)

# Remove very rare words (in < 5 articles): they carry little information
# but inflate the matrix considerably. We keep the untrimmed version (dtm_voll)
# for the dictionaries, because a rare word such as "Völkermord" should not
# drop out just because it occurs in fewer than 5 articles.
dtm <- dfm_trim(dtm_voll, min_docfreq = 5)

dtm   # shows dimensions (articles x words) and the share of zeros ("sparse")
```

```{r top-woerter}
# The most frequent words: a first plausibility check of whether the corpus "looks like the Middle East"
textstat_frequency(dtm, n = 30)
```

---

# Step 5: First substantive analyses

## 5.1 Dictionary approach: how often do certain terms occur?

A **dictionary** groups several words into one category. The `*` at the end is a
wildcard (`genozid*` matches “genozid”, “genozids”, “genozidal” …).

> **Important for interpretation:** The occurrence of “Genozid” (genocide) in an article does
> **not** mean that the outlet uses the term itself. It may be a quote (“Südafrika wirft Israel
> Genozid vor” (South Africa accuses Israel of genocide)) or a rejection. Dictionary counts are
> therefore only a **first indicator**. KWIC (5.2) and the sentence analysis (Step 6) clarify
> what lies behind them.

```{r woerterbuch}
diskurs_dict <- dictionary(list(
  genozid            = c("genozid*", "völkermord*", "voelkermord*"),
  terror             = c("terror*"),
  selbstverteidigung = c("selbstverteidigung*"),
  humanitaer         = c("humanitär*", "hunger*", "hilfslieferung*", "zivilist*"),
  kriegsverbrechen   = c("kriegsverbrechen*", "völkerrecht*", "voelkerrecht*"),
  antisemitismus     = c("antisemit*")
))

dict_dfm <- dfm_lookup(dtm_voll, diskurs_dict)

# Share of articles per week in which the category occurs at least once
dict_woche <- convert(dict_dfm, to = "data.frame") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(woche = floor_date(docvars(dict_dfm, "datum"), "week", week_start = 1)) |>
  group_by(woche) |>
  summarise(n_artikel = n(),
            across(all_of(names(diskurs_dict)), ~ mean(.x > 0)))

dict_woche
```

## 5.2 Keywords in context (KWIC): how is a term used?

KWIC shows each occurrence with the words before and after it. This is the key step
for moving from “occurs” to “**who** says **what**”. We work on the uncleaned tokens
so that the context remains readable.

```{r kwic}
toks_lesbar <- tokens(korp)
kwic(toks_lesbar, pattern = c("genozid*", "völkermord*"), window = 12) |> head(20)
```

---

# Step 6: Source attribution at sentence level

## The idea

A core question of your thesis: **to whom is a piece of information attributed**, and is it
flagged as **unverified**? In news texts, you can recognise this by typical patterns:

- “**nach Angaben der** israelischen Armee …” (according to the Israeli army)
- “**laut** dem von der Hamas kontrollierten Gesundheitsministerium …” (according to the
  Hamas-run health ministry)
- “… **teilte** die UN **mit**” (the UN announced), “… **zufolge**” (according to),
  “**wie** die IDF **erklärte**” (as the IDF stated)

And by **verification caveats**:

- “Die Angaben **lassen sich nicht unabhängig überprüfen**.” (The figures cannot be
  independently verified.)
- “**unabhängig bestätigt**” (independently confirmed), “**nicht verifiziert**” (not verified)

A DTM cannot capture this because it only counts whether words appear **anywhere in the
article**. We therefore split the texts into **sentences** and check each sentence:

1. Does it contain an **attribution pattern**?
2. Which **actor** is named?
3. Is there a **verification caveat** (in the same sentence or in the article)?

> This is a **rule-based first approximation**. For the thesis, you should validate it against
> a **hand-coded sample** (e.g. 300 sentences, ideally with a second coder) and report
> precision/recall. Later, it can be refined with NER (`spacyr`) or LLM-assisted annotation,
> which is then tested against the same sample.

```{r quellen-muster-de}
```

```{r funktion-saetze-markieren-de}
```

```{r quellen-saetze}
# Split texts into sentences. corpus_reshape() keeps the metadata.
saetze <- corpus_reshape(korp, to = "sentences")

satz_tab <- tibble(
  artikel_id = docvars(saetze, "artikel_id"),
  datum      = docvars(saetze, "datum"),
  satz       = as.character(saetze)
) |>
  saetze_markieren_de()   # attribution, verification, actors, health ministry (R/60_quellen.R)

# Result: how often is something attributed to each actor,
# and how often does a verification caveat appear in the same sentence?
satz_tab |>
  filter(zuschreibung) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(names(akteure_de)),
                   list(n = ~ sum(.x),
                        mit_verifikation = ~ sum(.x & verifikation)))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(),
                      names_to = c("akteur", ".value"),
                      names_pattern = "(.*)_(n|mit_verifikation)$")
```

```{r quellen-beispiele}
# As a check: random example sentences with attribution to the Israeli military.
# Read them! This quickly shows where the patterns are too broad or too narrow.
set.seed(42)
satz_tab |>
  filter(zuschreibung, israel_militaer) |>
  slice_sample(n = 10) |>
  pull(satz)
```

# Step 7: Template for further outlets

Each additional outlet needs only two things:

1. **A list of article URLs** for the period, obtained, depending on the site, via a search
   page, archive, sitemap (`/sitemap.xml`, often organised by date) or RSS feed. Always check
   `https://<seite>/robots.txt` first to see whether the relevant directory is disallowed.
2. **The CSS selector** for the body text (see Step 2).

What matters is that you end up with **the same columns** as for tagesschau. You can then
simply combine all outlets with `bind_rows()` and run the analyses above unchanged. `medium`
(outlet) becomes the central comparison variable.

> **For paywalled outlets (FAZ, NZZ, Spiegel, Welt …):** do not scrape; go through the
> library instead (Nexis Uni, Factiva, FAZ archive). You then read those exports into
> this format as well.

```{r vorlage-medium, eval = FALSE}
# TEMPLATE – check and adjust the selectors in the browser before use!
medium_scrapen <- function(urls, medium_name, selektor_text, selektor_titel = "h1",
                           selektor_datum = "time", pause = 3) {
  dir.create(file.path("data/raw", medium_name), showWarnings = FALSE)

  map_dfr(urls, function(u) {
    datei <- file.path("data/raw", medium_name, paste0(rlang::hash(u), ".html"))
    if (!file.exists(datei)) {
      Sys.sleep(pause)
      resp <- tryCatch(request(u) |> req_user_agent(kontakt) |> req_perform(),
                       error = function(e) NULL)
      if (is.null(resp)) return(NULL)
      writeLines(resp_body_string(resp), datei, useBytes = TRUE)
    }
    s <- read_html(datei, encoding = "UTF-8")
    tibble(
      medium = medium_name,
      id     = rlang::hash(u),
      url    = u,
      datum  = as.Date(ymd_hms(html_attr(html_element(s, selektor_datum), "datetime"),
                               quiet = TRUE)),
      titel  = html_text2(html_element(s, selektor_titel)),
      text   = paste(html_text2(html_elements(s, selektor_text)), collapse = "\n\n")
    )
  })
}

# Example call (the selector is a placeholder!):
# taz <- medium_scrapen(taz_urls, "taz", selektor_text = "article p")
# korpus_gesamt <- bind_rows(artikel, taz)
```

`sessionInfo()` documents the R and package versions. This belongs in the thesis appendix
so that the results can be reproduced.

```{r speichern}
saveRDS(list(korpus = korp, dtm = dtm, saetze = satz_tab),
        "data/processed/pilot_tagesschau.rds")
sessionInfo()
```

# What the pilot should tell you (checklist)

- [ ] **Duration:** How long did Steps 1 and 2 take? Extrapolate to all outlets and the full period.
- [ ] **Pre-filter:** How many articles does the pre-filter drop? Compare once with `vorfilter <- FALSE`.
- [ ] **Text quality:** Read 10 random texts. Are paragraphs missing, or are ads or navigation included?
- [ ] **Relevance filter:** Check a sample (see Step 3).
- [ ] **Dictionaries:** Do the KWIC hits make sense? Are terms missing?
- [ ] **Source patterns:** Read example sentences, note misclassifications and refine the patterns.

**Next steps afterwards:** literature review (framing, source use in crisis and war
journalism, text-as-data methods), sharpen the research questions and then add the second
outlet (e.g. taz).
